summary: The bill amends federal ethics law to bar Members of Congress, the President, Vice President, and their spouses and dependents from owning or trading stocks, commodities, futures, or similar investments, requiring divestment within 90 or 180 days and imposing a 10% fee plus profit forfeiture for violations.

scores.thoughts: The bill establishes ethics restrictions on stock ownership and trading by federal officials. It contains no provisions that authorize, appropriate, or modify any government expenditures or programs. Therefore, it has no bearing on government spending.

The bill incorporates section 1043 of the Internal Revenue Code to treat required divestitures as qualifying for certificates of divestiture (allowing nonrecognition of gain) and disallows tax deductions for losses arising from violations. These are narrow, mechanical uses of existing tax rules to facilitate compliance rather than any broad change to tax rates, brackets, or policy. The engagement is tangential and minor.
The bill addresses stock-trading restrictions for public officials and has no provisions related to health insurance, providers, Medicare/Medicaid, drug pricing, or any other healthcare matter.
No provisions in the bill address firearms, background checks, licensing, or gun rights.
The bill contains no language concerning visas, border security, asylum, deportation, or pathways to citizenship.
No provisions relate to reproductive health services, funding restrictions, or access to abortion.
The bill does not alter defense budgets, procurement, troop levels, or military policy.
No environmental regulations, emissions standards, land-use rules, or climate-related provisions appear in the bill.
The legislation does not modify eligibility, funding, or administration of welfare programs, SNAP, housing assistance, or similar safety-net programs.
No provisions address school funding, curriculum, student loans, school choice, or federal education policy.
The bill does not address controlled substances, decriminalization, enforcement priorities, or drug sentencing.
Penalties established by the bill are civil/administrative ethics sanctions (fees and disgorgement) enforced by ethics offices, not criminal sentencing reform or policing policy.

Although the bill defines terms such as “commodity” and “future,” these definitions serve only to delineate prohibited investments; the bill does not alter tariffs, trade agreements, import/export rules, or trade enforcement.
No provisions affect deficit levels, debt-ceiling adjustments, or fiscal targets.
The bill contains no language concerning nondiscrimination protections, marriage, gender-identity policies, or LGBTQ+ legal rights.
No provisions address foreign assistance, international development funding, or related appropriations.
The bill does not modify election administration, voter eligibility, campaign-finance disclosure, or voting access rules.
No provisions regulate data collection, platform liability, encryption, or technology-company oversight.
The bill does not address collective bargaining, union organizing, wage-and-hour rules, or employer obligations.
No provisions address religious exemptions, conscience protections, or conflicts between civil-rights statutes and religious exercise.
